topics.title: The Scaling Roadmap: Final Flow
topics.summary: Scale in order of cost and complexity: indexes, query tuning, cache, replicas, partitioning - and only then sharding.
topics.description:
When a database gets slow the temptation is to jump to the most "advanced" tool (sharding, microservices). The correct approach is to move through the cheap, high-impact steps first.

### The final flow
```
Single DB
   |
   v
Indexes
   |
   v
Query optimization
   |
   v
Redis (cache)
   |
   v
Read replicas
   |
   v
Partitioning
   |
   v
Only then -> Sharding
```

### Why this order
1. **Single DB** - start simple; one well-tuned database goes a long way.
2. **Indexes** - turn full scans into seeks; often a 100x win for one line of SQL.
3. **Query optimization** - fix N+1 queries, select only needed columns, paginate, use `EXPLAIN`.
4. **Redis / cache** - serve repeated reads from memory and lighten the DB.
5. **Read replicas** - copies of the database that handle read traffic; the primary handles writes.
6. **Partitioning** - split one huge table into smaller parts inside one database (by date, region...).
7. **Sharding** - split data across multiple database servers. Powerful but complex: cross-shard queries, rebalancing, operational pain.

### Rule of thumb
Every step adds operational cost. Measure first (slow query log, APM, EXPLAIN), fix the real bottleneck, and move to the next step only when the previous one is exhausted.
keyPoints: Order: indexes, query tuning, cache, replicas, partitioning, sharding
Measure before you scale
Each step adds complexity - take the cheapest one that works
Sharding is the last resort
pitfalls: Adding cache on top of un-indexed slow queries
Scaling without monitoring or load tests

examples.title: The ladder with typical tools
examples.code:
Step                 Tool / action                       Cost
-------------------  ----------------------------------  ------
1 Indexes            CREATE INDEX, EXPLAIN               low
2 Query tuning       fix N+1, LIMIT, projections         low
3 Cache              Redis, CDN                          medium
4 Read replicas      primary + N replicas                medium
5 Partitioning       table partitions by date/range      medium
6 Sharding           split data across DB servers        high
examples.explanation: Climb one rung at a time.

interview.q: What would you do first if the database is slow?
interview.a: Find the slow queries, check indexes and execution plans, fix inefficient queries; then consider caching.

interview.q: Why is sharding the last step?
interview.a: It makes queries, transactions and operations much more complex, so it is only worthwhile when a single primary (even with replicas) cannot handle the write volume or data size.

topics.title: Load Balancer & Connection Pools
topics.summary: Spread traffic over many API servers and protect the database by reusing a limited number of connections.
topics.description:
Imagine **1M users** hitting your service. One server cannot handle them, so you run many copies of the API behind a **load balancer**.

### Flow
```
1M users
   |
   v
Load Balancer
   |
   v
100 API servers
   |
   v
Connection pools
   |
   v
Database
```

### Load balancer
Receives every request and forwards it to a healthy server (Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB, Cloudflare).
* **Algorithms**: round robin, least connections, IP hash.
* **Health checks** remove dead servers automatically.
* Enables **zero-downtime deploys** and horizontal scaling: add servers, no code change.
* Requires **stateless** servers - sessions and files must live in Redis / object storage, not on one machine.

### Connection pooling
Opening a database connection is expensive and a database can only hold a limited number (e.g. 100-500). 100 API servers each opening 20 connections would crush it. A **pool** keeps a small set of open connections that requests borrow and return. Tools: pool settings in your driver/ORM, **PgBouncer** for PostgreSQL, ProxySQL for MySQL.

### Sizing
Total connections = servers x pool size per server. Keep it below the database limit.
keyPoints: Load balancer distributes requests and health-checks servers
Servers must be stateless to scale horizontally
Connection pools reuse a small set of DB connections
servers x pool size must stay under the DB limit
pitfalls: Storing sessions or uploads on the local disk of one server
Opening a new DB connection per request
Huge pool sizes on every server

examples.title: Nginx upstream (sketch)
examples.explanation: Nginx sends each request to the server with the fewest active connections.

examples.title: Pool in Node (pg)
examples.explanation: The pool lends one of 10 connections per query and takes it back.

interview.q: Why must app servers be stateless?
interview.a: So any server can handle any request; otherwise the load balancer would need sticky sessions and you could not add or remove servers freely.
Creating connections is slow and databases limit them; pooling reuses connections and caps the load.

topics.title: Redis: Cache, Sessions, Rate Limits & More
topics.summary: Redis is a very fast in-memory data store used for caching, sessions, rate limiting, counters, locks, temporary data and light queues.
topics.description:
**Redis** keeps data in RAM, so reads and writes take microseconds. It is rarely the primary database; it sits **next to** it and takes pressure off.

### What it is used for
| Use | How |
|---|---|
| **Cache** | store query results / pages with a TTL |
| **Sessions** | shared session store for many servers |
| **Rate limiting** | counter per IP/user with expiry (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) |
| **Counters** | likes, views, stock counters (atomic `INCR`) |
| **Locks** | distributed locks (`SET key value NX PX 30000`) |
| **Temporary data** | OTPs, password-reset tokens, short-lived state |
| **Queue support** | lists, streams and BullMQ job queues |
| **Leaderboards** | sorted sets |

### Data types
Strings, hashes, lists, sets, **sorted sets**, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog.

### Important traits
* Single-threaded command execution -> operations are atomic.
* **TTL** on keys for automatic expiry.
* Persistence is optional (RDB snapshots, AOF log); memory is the limit, so choose an **eviction policy** (e.g. `allkeys-lru`).
* Scales with replication, Sentinel (failover) and Cluster (sharding).
keyPoints: In-memory, microsecond latency
Used for cache, sessions, rate limits, counters, locks, temp data, queues
Keys can expire with a TTL
Atomic operations like INCR make counters and limits safe
Set an eviction policy because RAM is limited
pitfalls: Treating Redis as the only copy of important data
Using `KEYS *` in production (blocks the server) - use `SCAN`

examples.title: Fixed-window rate limiter
examples.explanation: One counter per user per minute that expires on its own.

examples.title: Redis commands
examples.code:
SET session:abc '{"userId":42}' EX 3600
GET session:abc
INCR page:views
ZADD leaderboard 1500 "asha"
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
examples.explanation: Session with an hour TTL, a counter and a leaderboard.

interview.a: Data lives in memory and it uses efficient single-threaded event-loop processing with simple data structures.

interview.q: How would you implement rate limiting with Redis?
interview.a: Use a key per client and time window, increment it atomically, set an expiry on the first hit and reject when the count exceeds the limit.

topics.title: Message Queues & Background Workers
topics.summary: Move slow or non-critical work (email, search indexing, analytics) off the request path with a queue and workers.
topics.description:
Some tasks should **not** run inside the HTTP request: sending e-mails, resizing images, processing a resume, updating a search index. A **queue** lets the API respond immediately while **workers** process jobs in the background.

### Architecture
```
API
 |
 v
Kafka / RabbitMQ / SQS / BullMQ
 |
 |-- Email worker
 |-- Notification worker
 |-- Search indexing worker
 |-- Recommendation worker
 |-- Analytics pipeline
 +-- Resume processing worker
```

### Why queues
* **Faster responses** - the API only enqueues a job.
* **Resilience** - if a worker is down the jobs wait; failed jobs are **retried**.
* **Smoothing spikes** - the queue absorbs bursts, workers consume at their pace.
* **Decoupling** - producers do not know consumers; add new workers without touching the API.

### Choosing a tool
* **BullMQ** (Redis based) - easy job queue for Node.js with retries, delays, priorities.
* **RabbitMQ** - classic message broker with routing.
* **SQS** - managed AWS queue.
* **Kafka** - distributed log for very high throughput event streaming; many consumers can replay events.

### Design rules
Make jobs **idempotent** (running twice is harmless), add retries with back-off and a **dead-letter queue** for jobs that keep failing.
keyPoints: The API enqueues, workers process asynchronously
Queues add retries, buffering and decoupling
BullMQ/RabbitMQ/SQS for jobs, Kafka for event streams
Jobs must be idempotent
Use a dead-letter queue for poison messages
pitfalls: Doing slow work inside the request handler
Non-idempotent jobs that double-charge or double-email on retry

examples.title: BullMQ producer and worker
examples.explanation: 202 Accepted tells the client the work was queued but not finished.

interview.a: To make slow work asynchronous, absorb traffic spikes, retry failures and decouple services.
RabbitMQ is a broker that delivers messages to consumers and removes them; Kafka is a persistent distributed log that supports very high throughput and replaying events.

topics.title: Replication & Sharding
topics.summary: Replication copies the same data to several servers; sharding splits the data so each server holds a part.
topics.description:
These two ideas are often confused. They solve **different** problems.

### Replication - same data, many copies
A **primary** (leader) accepts writes and streams changes to **replicas** (followers).
* Scales **reads** (send SELECTs to replicas).
* Gives **high availability**: if the primary dies, a replica is promoted (failover).
* Backups can run on a replica.
* Caveat: **replication lag** - a replica may be a few milliseconds behind, so a user may not immediately see their own write (read-your-writes problem).

### Sharding - split the data
Sharding = breaking one very large database into **multiple smaller databases** so that load and data are distributed over several machines.
* Scales **writes** and **total storage**.
* A **shard key** decides where a row lives, e.g. `user_id % 4`, a hash range, or region.
* Good keys give an even spread; bad keys create **hot shards**.

```
Replication:  Primary --> Replica 1
                      \-> Replica 2        (all hold ALL data)

Sharding:     Shard A: users 1..1M
              Shard B: users 1M..2M         (each holds PART of data)
              Shard C: users 2M..3M
```

### Cost of sharding
Cross-shard JOINs and transactions are hard, re-sharding is painful, and every query needs routing. That is why it comes last in the scaling roadmap. In practice you combine both: each shard has its own replicas.
keyPoints: Replication = copies for read scale and availability
Sharding = splitting data for write scale and size
Replication lag causes stale reads
The shard key must spread load evenly
Large systems use both: shards with replicas
pitfalls: Choosing a monotonic shard key (like timestamp) that creates a hot shard
Sharding before indexes, caching and replicas

examples.title: Routing by shard key
examples.explanation: Simple modulo routing. Production systems prefer consistent hashing so adding a shard moves few keys.

interview.a: Replication duplicates all data across servers (reads, availability); sharding partitions data across servers (writes, capacity).
A shard that receives a disproportionate share of traffic because of an uneven shard key distribution.

topics.title: Search Engines: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr
topics.summary: Dedicated search engines build inverted indexes for fast full-text search, ranking and filtering at scale.
topics.description:
A relational database is poor at searches like "find products matching *wireless headphones* with typos, sorted by relevance". A **search engine** is built for exactly this.

### Tools
* **Elasticsearch** - most popular, built on Lucene, REST/JSON API.
* **OpenSearch** - AWS-led fork of Elasticsearch.
* **Solr** - mature Lucene-based server from Apache.
* **Lucene** - the Java library underneath all of them.

### How it works: inverted index
Instead of "document -> words", it stores "word -> documents".

```
doc1: "red running shoes"
doc2: "blue running jacket"

running -> [doc1, doc2]
shoes   -> [doc1]
jacket  -> [doc2]
```

Lookups are fast and results are **scored** by relevance (TF-IDF / BM25).

### Features
Full-text search, typo tolerance (fuzzy), autocomplete, synonyms, facets/filters, aggregations, geo search.

### How it fits into the system
The search engine is **not** the source of truth. Your primary DB stays authoritative; a **search indexing worker** consumes change events from a queue and updates the index. Search results return ids which you can hydrate from the database if needed.
keyPoints: Built on inverted indexes (word -> documents)
Relevance scoring and fuzzy matching out of the box
Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr all build on Lucene
Keep the primary DB as the source of truth
Update the index asynchronously via queue workers
pitfalls: Using SQL `LIKE '%term%'` for real search at scale
Using the search engine as the only data store
Forgetting to re-index after schema/mapping changes

examples.title: Elasticsearch query
examples.explanation: A typo tolerant text search combined with a price filter.

interview.q: Why not use SQL LIKE for search?
interview.a: A leading wildcard cannot use a normal index, so it scans the table, and it has no relevance ranking, stemming or typo tolerance.
A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, enabling fast full-text lookups.
